captions.text: Right, let's crack on. Last week we did the mean, and I said the mean is a bit of a blunt instrument. Today we look at spread, how far the data wanders from the centre.

Picture two classes. Both average sixty-five percent. In Class A everyone scored between sixty and seventy. In Class B, scores go from twenty all the way up to a hundred. Same mean, completely different story.
The quickest measure is the range: max minus min. It's a ballpark figure, handy on the back of an envelope, but one outlier and it goes out the window.

So we want something that uses every data point. Enter the variance. For each observation x i, we take the deviation from the sample mean, x bar, square it, add them all up, and divide by n minus one.

Now, why n minus one and not n? This is Bessel's correction. Because we estimate x bar from the same sample, we lose one degree of freedom, and dividing by n would systematically underestimate the population variance. Dividing by n minus one makes it an unbiased estimator.
If that went a bit over your head, don't panic, it's bread and butter for next week's lecture on estimators.

Problem with variance: the units are squared. If your data's in pounds, variance is in pounds squared, which nobody can interpret. So we take the square root and get the standard deviation, back in the original units.

Quick example. Scores four, six, eight. Mean is six. Deviations are minus two, zero, plus two. Square them, four, zero, four, sum is eight. Divide by n minus one, that's two, variance is four, standard deviation is two.

Rule of thumb: for roughly normal data, about sixty-eight percent of observations fall within one standard deviation of the mean. That's the empirical rule, and we'll lean on it heavily when we get to confidence intervals.
Right, that's the gist. For the problem sheet, have a crack at questions one to four before Thursday's tutorial. Cheers, everyone.

terms.explanation: How far the data values are scattered around the centre (the mean).
terms.example: Class B (20 to 100) has a bigger spread than Class A (60 to 70).

terms.explanation: The largest value minus the smallest value.
A value far away from the rest of the data, which can distort a summary.
terms.example: One student scoring 2 in a class of 60-70s.

terms.explanation: The average squared distance of each value from the mean. Bigger variance means more spread.
The symbol for the mean of the sample.
Dividing by n - 1 instead of n when computing sample variance, so the estimate is not too small on average.
terms.example: For 3 scores, divide the sum of squares by 2, not 3.

terms.explanation: The number of values that are free to vary. Using the sample mean uses up one, leaving n - 1.
terms.example: If 3 numbers must average 6, once you pick two, the third is fixed.

terms.explanation: A formula that gets the true population value right on average, over many samples.
terms.example: Sample variance with n - 1 is unbiased for the population variance.

terms.explanation: The square root of the variance, in the same units as the data.
For roughly bell-shaped data, about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean.
terms.example: Mean 65, SD 5: about 68% of students score 60 to 70.

terms.term: crack on / have a crack at
terms.explanation: British informal: 'crack on' means start or continue; 'have a crack at' means try.
A tool that works roughly but misses detail.

terms.term: ballpark figure / back of an envelope
terms.explanation: A rough estimate, done quickly without precision.
A practical rule that is usually roughly right.

lecturer_insights.room_status: About 30% of the room got lost at 01:08 on why we divide by n − 1. Everything else is mostly fine.

clusters.label: Why divide by n − 1?
clusters.transcript_quote: This is Bessel's correction... we lose one degree of freedom
clusters.suggestion: Try: 'Our data is closer to its own mean than to the true mean, so dividing by n makes the spread look too small. n − 1 nudges it back up.' Then show 3 numbers averaging 6: pick two, the third is forced. That's the lost degree of freedom.

clusters.label: What does 'unbiased' mean?
clusters.suggestion: Say: 'Unbiased means right on average. If 1,000 students each took a sample, their n − 1 variances would average out to the true variance.' Confirm that the full proof is next week.

clusters.label: Squared units and why square
clusters.suggestion: Explain: 'We square so negatives don't cancel positives. Squaring also squares the units, which is why we take the square root to get SD.' Mention absolute deviation exists but is harder to work with mathematically.

language_flags.phrase: ballpark figure / back of an envelope
language_flags.suggestion: Say 'rough estimate' once alongside the idiom.

key_points: The mean alone hides how spread out data is.
Range (max − min) is quick but sensitive to outliers.
Variance averages the squared deviations from the mean; for a sample, divide by n − 1.
Standard deviation is the square root of variance, in the original units.
For roughly normal data, about 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean.

formulas.symbols: s² sample variance, xᵢ each value, x̄ sample mean, n number of values
